title: Scam 1992 — Why India's Best-Rated Web Series Is About a Stockbroker
excerpt: A ten-episode series about a 1990s securities fraud became India's highest-rated show. How Scam 1992 pulled that off.
author: StarScoop Daily Staff
imageAlt: Scam 1992 The Harshad Mehta Story backdrop — SonyLIV web series
metaDescription: Scam 1992 explained — how a SonyLIV series about a stockbroker became India's highest-rated web series. Cast, story, and where to watch.
content:
A ten-episode series about a securities fraud from the early 1990s, on a platform most people outside India have never heard of, became one of the highest-rated shows anywhere.

Scam 1992: The Harshad Mehta Story holds a 4.2/5 TMDB rating and is routinely cited as the best Indian web series ever made. Here's why it works.

What It's About

The series follows Harshad Mehta, a stockbroker from a modest Mumbai background who rose to dominate the Indian stock market before the mechanism behind his rise collapsed into one of the country's largest financial scandals.

The scam itself involved exploiting gaps in how banks settled government securities — money that should have moved between institutions instead moved into the market.

If that sounds dry, that's the point. The show's central achievement is making bank receipts and settlement periods genuinely tense.

📺 SonyLIV · 1 season · 10 episodes · Status: Ended · TMDB: 4.2/5

Pratik Gandhi's Performance Carries It

Pratik Gandhi came from Gujarati theatre and was largely unknown to a national audience before this. That anonymity turned out to be an asset — there was no star persona sitting between the actor and the character.

The performance works because it refuses to settle on a verdict. Mehta is charming, genuinely brilliant, and doing something indefensible, and Gandhi plays all three without signalling which one you should weigh most.

Supporting him: Shreya Dhanwanthary as the journalist who broke the story, plus Satish Kaushik, Hemant Kher, Anjali Barot and K.K. Raina.

Dhanwanthary's role matters structurally — the journalist thread gives the audience someone outside the scheme to follow, which is what stops the series becoming an unbroken celebration of the man at its centre.

Why the Financial Detail Is the Point

Most dramas about finance simplify the mechanics on the assumption audiences won't follow. Scam 1992 does the opposite — it explains the actual instruments, and trusts you to keep up.

That decision is why it works. The tension comes from understanding precisely how exposed Mehta is at any moment. Without the mechanics you have a story about a man who got rich and then didn't.

It also sidesteps the usual trap of this genre. Films about financial crime often end up glamorising the criminal, because wealth looks good on screen and the victims are abstract. Scam 1992 keeps returning to the fact that the money came from somewhere — ordinary investors, and public institutions.

Director Hansal Mehta has a long record with real-events material and treats the period seriously: the newsrooms, the trading floor, the technology, all specific rather than generically retro.

What It Proved About Indian Streaming

Its success made an argument that ran against the prevailing formula.

When it arrived, Indian streaming's dominant genre was violent small-town crime — the register our Mirzapur breakdown covers. Scam 1992 had no violence, no stars, and a subject most executives would call uncommercial.

It outperformed most of that slate anyway, on a smaller budget, and did it on SonyLIV rather than Netflix or Prime Video — proving a smaller platform could break out with the right show.

Combined with Panchayat's success in an entirely different register, the lesson is fairly clear: Indian audiences will follow quality regardless of genre, and the assumed formula was narrower than the audience actually is.

Should You Watch It?

Yes, and it's a short commitment — ten episodes, one season, complete. No ongoing series to keep up with.

You don't need any finance background. The show teaches you what you need as it goes, which is a large part of the pleasure.

Worth knowing going in: it is dialogue-heavy and paced deliberately. If you want action, this isn't it. If you want a genuinely gripping character study with real stakes, few Indian series come close.

The theme music has also become independently famous in India — you will recognise it even if you have never seen the show.
